verdicts.reason: Distinct from the catalogue: states-of-matter only shows ice less dense than water inside a molecular box, and flight is about lift, not buoyancy. Level 0 is honest (KS3 upthrust, PhET Buoyancy Basics), and the model (Archimedes with a waterline from a hull's cross-section) is easily buildable. Handbook densities are facts. Note for the curator: the pool also has sink-or-float (chemistry) and fluid-pressure-buoyancy (physics), so these are probably to be merged or chosen between. Two factual faults. (1) The takeaway says a thing floats when it pushes aside MORE than its own weight. A floating object pushes aside exactly its own weight. The rule is that it floats if it can push aside its own weight before it is completely under, and as written the takeaway invites the opposite misconception. (2) A 'scale under the tank' does not show the pushed-aside water: for a stone resting on the bottom, it rises by the stone's whole weight. The honest instrument is an overflow (eureka) can spilling into a cup on a scale, set beside a spring balance holding the object.

fixed.takeaway: A thing floats if it can push aside its own weight of water (or air) before it is completely under, which is why the same lump of clay sinks as a ball and floats as a bowl.
fixed.interaction: Lower objects into a brim-full tank (a stone, an apple, a wooden block, a steel ball, a ball of modelling clay): the water each one pushes aside spills into a cup on a scale, and a spring balance holding the object shows it getting lighter as it goes in. Each one sinks, or settles where the spilled water weighs as much as it does. Reshape the clay from a ball into a bowl and the same lump floats; load it with marbles until it goes under. Change the water to salt water or to oil and see who floats now; finally warm the air inside a balloon and watch it rise through the surrounding air the same way.

verdicts.reason: Distinct from electromagnetism (level 2: charges, field lines, induction), and squarely NGSS 3-PS2-3 / KS2 Year 3. Level 0 is honest. The Gilbert two-pole model with inverse-square pole forces, a field-direction field for the filings and compass, and an induced dipole in steel is a real, cheap model; it needs no data. Note for the curator: the pool also has magnets-and-electromagnets (physics) and compass-and-magnetic-poles (earth), which overlap at this level. The fault is the pitfall: 'only iron, steel, nickel and cobalt' repeats a misconception. Common austenitic stainless steels (304/316, cutlery and sinks) are not attracted or only barely, while many alloys and some rare-earth metals are. The takeaway and the cut-magnet point are correct.

fixed.pitfall: A magnet does not attract all metals, nor even all steel: it pulls iron, nickel, cobalt and most steels, but not aluminium, copper, gold or many stainless-steel spoons and sinks. And cutting a magnet never separates its poles: each piece has two.

verdicts.reason: Nothing in the catalogue runs a reaction-diffusion PDE. chaos-fractals iterates maps, and morphogen-gradients and segmentation-clock are separate pool proposals. A 2D activator-inhibitor grid (Gierer-Meinhardt or Schnakenberg) runs at interactive rates on the client. Level 3 is honest: Turing instability and its diffusion-ratio condition are taught in university mathematical biology (Murray). The diffusion-ratio threshold, the stripes inserted as the domain grows (Kondo & Asai 1995, Pomacanthus) and the spots that turn to bands on a tapering tail are standard results, and the pitfall about contested cases is sound. Two small corrections. The wavelength is set by the reaction rates together with the two diffusion coefficients, not by 'rates alone'. The angelfish case is itself debated (Painter, Maini & Othmer 1999 add cell movement), so the pitfall should hedge it.

fixed.takeaway: Two chemicals, one that makes more of itself and a faster-spreading one that suppresses it, can turn a uniform field into regular spots or stripes with no blueprint, at a spacing set by their reaction and diffusion rates.
fixed.pitfall: Not every stripe in nature is a Turing pattern. The page should name where a Turing-type mechanism is well supported (digit spacing, hair and feather follicles) and where the evidence is mixed (fish skin, where pigment cells also move). It must not claim the mechanism for zebra stripes or fingerprints without saying that is contested.

verdicts.reason: It is distinct from the catalogue (states-of-matter changes one substance's phase), but it nearly duplicates the pool candidate dissolving-sugar: a particle counter, warming, a saturation limit, nothing lost. Its dry-it-back step overlaps separating-mixtures (the evaporating dish) and growing-crystals. The takeaway is also wrong for half the page. Salt's solubility barely changes with temperature (about 35.7 to 39 g per 100 g of water from 0 to 100 °C), while sucrose's rises from about 179 to 487 g. So 'warm water takes more' holds for sugar only. 'Until no more will fit' teaches the misconception that saturation means running out of room between water particles. The fix narrows the page to what neither sibling shows: sugar and salt side by side, and how differently temperature affects them. It should be merged with dissolving-sugar, or that one dropped.

fixed.interaction: Two glasses of water drawn as particles, one for sugar and one for salt, and a spoonful counter under each. One control at a time: tip in another spoonful, then slide the thermometer to warm both glasses. Each grain breaks into particles that wander off among the water particles until the water will take no more, and the rest sits on the bottom. Warming lets the sugar glass take spoonful after spoonful more, while the salt glass hardly takes any extra. At the end, let the water dry away and watch the same particles gather back into grains.
fixed.takeaway: Dissolved sugar and salt have not vanished: their particles are spread among the water's, each glass of water takes only so much, and warming lets it take far more sugar but hardly any more salt.
fixed.pitfall: Dissolving is not melting, and the sugar does not disappear or turn into water: every particle is still there, which is why the water tastes sweet and weighs more. A full glass is not 'out of room' between water particles: it stops because dissolving and grains re-forming have come into balance.
fixed.overlapWith: dissolving-sugar (pool) and states-of-matter: states-of-matter changes the phase of one substance. This page compares two solids and shows that temperature raises how much sugar water will take but barely changes salt. It should be merged with dissolving-sugar rather than built alongside it.
fixed.needs: Solubility of sucrose and of sodium chloride in water from 0 to 100 °C (about a dozen values) from the IUPAC-NIST Solubility Data Series, freely readable at NIST, or the ACS Middle School Chemistry tables; published facts, no dataset licence to clear.
fixed.needsSource: About a dozen tabulated solubility values (IUPAC-NIST Solubility Data Series via NIST; ACS Middle School Chemistry, chapter 5 lesson 6); facts, no licence needed.

verdicts.reason: No catalogue page covers freezing-point depression or freezing mixtures: states-of-matter covers only pure substances. Its level-0 framing works without formulas, using temperatures only as comparisons. The data source is real and public domain: FHWA-RD-95-202, Appendix B (freezing points of chemical solutions), is a US government work. The physics is right. NaCl brine's lowest freezing point is about −21 °C, the bath cools because melting absorbs heat, and the pitfall is correct. The one gap is that the interaction does not name its model. The honest model is the brine freezing-point curve plus a heat balance between ice, brine and cream, with the particle picture as illustration. A small edit makes that explicit and replaces the vague 'turn the cold down'.

fixed.interaction: A block of ice drawn as a neat stack of water particles, with a thermometer. One control at a time: sprinkle salt, and salt particles get between the water particles at the surface so the stack cannot re-form, and the ice melts although the thermometer reads below freezing. Set the weather colder and the salt stops working; pour on more salt and see the point where extra salt no longer helps. Then put a bag of cream into the salted ice: the melting pulls heat out of the cream, the bath's thermometer drops below what plain ice could reach, and the cream freezes. Behind the picture runs the measured freezing-point curve of salt water and a running count of the heat that melting takes from the bath and the cream.

verdicts.reason: It is distinct from entropy, levelled honestly for KS2 (Year 5 lists thermal conductivity among material properties), and buildable as 1D heat conduction between skin and object. The physics, though, is stated wrongly in two places. First, what sets the felt temperature is the contact temperature, which depends on each material's thermal effusivity sqrt(k·ρ·c) (conductivity, density and heat capacity together), not on conductivity alone. Physics-teaching papers flag 'conducts heat away faster' as the misleading version, so the model must use effusivity, even though the page never says the word. Second, metal feels hottest only when the room is warmer than the skin (above about 33 °C), not merely 'hot'.

fixed.interaction: A table with a metal spoon, a wooden spoon, a plastic cup and a woollen glove, all at room temperature, with a thermometer that reads the same on each. Drag a finger onto any one: a strip of heat colour flows out of the fingertip into the object, fast into the metal and barely at all into the wool, and a 'feels like' dial follows the temperature where skin meets object. One control: the room temperature. Warm the room past the temperature of your hand and the order flips, so the same metal now feels hottest. The flow is a heat-conduction model in which each material uses its real conductivity, density and heat capacity.
fixed.takeaway: Everything on the table is the same temperature; the metal feels cold because it draws heat out of your finger fastest, and when the room is warmer than your hand the same metal feels hottest.
fixed.needs: Thermal conductivity, density and specific heat of skin, a metal (steel or aluminium), wood, plastic and wool: under twenty published constants from textbook tables or Wikipedia's material-property tables (CC BY-SA). The model combines them, because contact temperature depends on all three.
fixed.pitfall: Metal is not colder than wood, and cold does not flow into your hand: heat flows out of it, and a thermometer shows the two objects equal. The page also should not say conductivity alone decides it: how much heat the material soaks up per degree matters too.

verdicts.reason: Nothing in the catalogue covers dislocations (bridges-structures stays at the scale of members). Level 3 is honest: dislocation glide and solid-solution strengthening are core university materials science (MIT 3.012, MITx 3.012S.3x). A 2D Lennard-Jones crystal of a few hundred to a few thousand atoms is buildable on the client: states-of-matter already runs 2D molecular dynamics, and Bailey, Sethna and Myers simulate an edge dislocation in a 2D Lennard-Jones crystal. Three problems need fixing. (a) The takeaway's 'a thousand times below' cannot be observed in the graphic: a small 2D Lennard-Jones toy shows a large gap, but not the factor of 100 to 10,000 of real metals. The number belongs in the text, not the takeaway. (b) Work hardening by multiplying dislocations needs dislocation sources and large boxes; the honest small-box version is a pile-up against an obstacle. (c) newtons-laws is an unhelpful prerequisite. The crystal lattice comes from semiconductors ('Crystals & semiconductors') and the atom-box simulation from states-of-matter.

fixed.interaction: Shear a two-dimensional crystal of simulated atoms that contains an edge dislocation, and watch the defect glide one row of bonds at a time while a gauge shows the stress it took. Remove the dislocation, and the perfect crystal holds to a far higher stress before a whole plane slips at once. Sprinkle in larger or smaller foreign atoms and the dislocation snags on them, so the gauge must climb higher before it moves. Add a second and third dislocation and drive them against a row of obstacles, where they pile up and resist further slip.
fixed.takeaway: A crystal with a dislocation yields at a small fraction of the stress a perfect crystal needs, because the defect breaks one row of bonds at a time, and foreign atoms raise that stress by pinning it.
fixed.needs: None beyond a 2D Lennard-Jones pair potential, the same kind of model states-of-matter runs. Solute atoms are modelled as particles with a larger or smaller size parameter.
